accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS RL.2.2 (recount fables and folktales from diverse cultures and determine their central message, lesson or moral) and RL.3.2 (explain how the message is conveyed through key details), and the England KS1 and LKS2 reading programmes of study. Story facts were checked against standard retellings: Aesop's Tortoise and the Hare, Ant and the Grasshopper, Lion and the Mouse and Boy Who Cried Wolf; the Ashanti tale of Anansi hiding wisdom in a pot until his son Ntikuma suggests carrying it on his back; and the Panchatantra Monkey and Crocodile, where the monkey says his heart is in the tree.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips in identifying theme: giving a plot summary as the moral (the tortoise-won prediction, event cards and the Sam item), naming the topic (lions are big, ants work hard), stating a moral so narrowly it fits only one character (the wolf sort and narrow challenge tag), choosing true but irrelevant details as support (tree and long-ears cards), and looking for the lesson in the title or first line.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmoral is about how a fable's message is built and proved: a fixed moral banner with five detail cards where only action details count as proof, a three-row choice, result, lesson chain, a gap that only the life rule fills for tales from Greece, Ghana and India, and an everyone versus only-this-story sort. The shingle gate passed against every lab, including flagtale, flagpurp and flagevid.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers by trying that an event card is refused from the lesson box, that the tree and ears cards are turned down as proof while what the animals do is accepted, and that the lesson card cannot go before the choice. Three different tales then show the same rule-for-life pattern, and the wolf sort turns a narrow rule into a general one.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: the tortoise won the race as the lesson, the first line of the story as the source of the lesson, and the mouse chewed a net as the moral of The Lion and the Mouse. The sort refuses the event card, the chain shows choice then result then lesson, and the gap rejects the net card before the done message echoes the prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with eight tagged wrong-answer messages (event, topic, place, looks, narrow, opposite, title, first). Each names the slip, for example that only fits the boy so say it so it helps anyone, or the story shows the opposite because the little mouse saves the lion.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid paragraphs score about FK 1.3 against the 5.0 target with short sentences and the words fable, moral, lesson and key details; adult paragraphs score about FK 9.3 against 10.0 while keeping the precise terms central message, recount, folktale and key details with RL.2.2 and RL.3.2.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and explanation overlap under 12 percent, including against Simple stories with a beginning and an ending and Why the author wrote it. Each adult paragraph carries curriculum references, defined vocabulary, named mistakes or what the lab does, and item explanations say why the wrong options are events or facts.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop. Screenshots at 390 px in light and dark themes show the detail cards in two columns with wrapped text, the chain as three full-width rows, folktale text readable in its panel, and three option cards with wrapped lines; every action has a full-width button below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with every spoken message, every drag or tap has a labelled button (for example Key detail? The hare naps under a tree), canvas text uses the theme text colour on pale tiles in light mode and slate in dark mode, and reduced motion shortens auto-play delays.

sources: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts: RL.2.2 and RL.3.2 (Key Ideas and Details)
DfE (2013) English programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, Year 2 and Years 3-4 reading comprehension
Aesop's Fables (Gibbs translation, Oxford World's Classics, 2002): The Tortoise and the Hare, The Ant and the Grasshopper, The Lion and the Mouse, The Boy Who Cried Wolf
Ashanti folktale: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom (as retold in Library of Congress and Ghanaian school collections)
Panchatantra, Book 4: The Monkey and the Crocodile
